summary: A 1975 extension to FTP for transferring files in page mode between TENEX systems. It also discusses how reliable such file transfers are. It updates RFC 354.

eli5.summary: TENEX computers stored files in fixed-size pages. This note lets two of them send files page by page instead of as one long stream.

questions: how did tenex transfer paged files over ftp
what is in an xtp chunk header
subtitle: How TENEX sites got FTP to send whole paged files, holes and all, with checksums and sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: TENEX stores files as a page table pointing at 512-word pages, with gaps and an end-of-file pointer that can sit anywhere. FTP had no way to move such files, and the author also wanted network transfers to be checksummed.
tldr.mechanism: A new experimental TYPE called XTP sends the file as numbered chunks. Each chunk has a six-word header (checksum, sequence number, data word count, page number, access bits, chunk type) followed by a data page or the file descriptor block.
tldr.outcome: It was running on all the BBN systems and some other sites. The author calls the single-TYPE approach incorrect and hopes a proper design will be negotiated in the NEW protocol (RFC 542).

today: RFC 683 is dated April 1975 and updates RFC 354; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no later RFC replacing it. It is best read as a snapshot of one site's experimental FTP extension.

sections.title: The Problems and the Choices Made
sections.content:
RFC 683 extends the "OLD" FTP protocol (RFC 354) so TENEX paged files can cross the network. The author is open that this is not necessarily the correct design: a correct one was to be negotiated in the "NEW" protocol (RFC 542), if funding appeared.

Two problems are attacked. One is network reliability: the author wants a checksummed, block-sequence-numbered mode, ideally with data compression as well. The other is that TENEX disk files do not fit FTP, which is the motivation here, because NLS data files need it.

Done properly, these would be new MODEs and a new STRUcture. Instead the author implemented everything as one new TYPE, partly because that meant less surgery on the FTP user and server programs.
sections.eli5: The author wanted two things: a way to check that pages arrive intact, and a way to send oddly shaped files. The quickest fix was one new setting, even though he admits a tidier one might exist.

sections.title: What a TENEX Disk File Looks Like
sections.content:
A TENEX file has four parts: a pathname, a page table, a possibly empty set of pages, and a set of attributes kept in the FDB (File Descriptor Block). The page table holds up to 2**18 entries. Each entry is either empty or points to a page, and each non-empty entry has its own access bits.

A page is a contiguous set of 512 words of 36 bits each. Pages need not be contiguous in the table, so a file can have empty slots between occupied ones. The end-of-file pointer is just a number and need not point at the last datum. Both of these oddities occur with NLS data files.
sections.eli5: Imagine a notebook with some pages torn out and a bookmark that is not on the last page. To copy it faithfully you must remember which pages are missing and where the bookmark is.

sections.title: TYPE XTP and the Chunk Format
sections.content:
The new TYPE is named XTP. The author proposes the pattern for all key letters: "X" means experimental (agreed between cooperating sites), the next letter is signed out to an implementor for a system ("T" for TENEX), and the rest distinguish private values ("P" for Paged). XTP is only implemented for STRU F, BYTE 36 and MODE S.

Data travels in chunks. A chunk starts with a word holding the number of header words that follow, currently 6, then those six words, then the data words. The six header words are:

  • Word 1: a one's complement checksum over the six header words and the data words; the sum including the checksum must come out plus or minus zero.
  • Word 2: a sequence number, starting at 1.
  • Word 3: NDW, the number of data words after the header.
  • Word 4: the page number in the file's page map; holes are simply not sent, and a hole is not a page of zeroes.
  • Word 5: the access bits for the page.
  • Word 6: the chunk type, currently 0 for a data page and -3 for an FDB.

NDW is 1000 octal for a data page and 25 octal for an FDB. Trailing zeroes in a page may later be dropped, and receivers accept such shortened pages.
sections.eli5: Each page goes into an envelope with a label: a check number, a count, which page it is, and what kind of thing is inside. Pages that were never there are just not mailed.

sections.title: Verification and Closing Comments
sections.content:
An error is reported if the checksum fails, if the sequence number is not correct, if NDW is unreasonable for the chunk type, or if the network file ends anywhere other than right after the data of an FDB chunk. So the FDB comes last.

The author says the FTP server and user were in operation on all the BBN systems and some other sites. He thinks checksumming and sequencing should be addressed in the NEW protocol, and describes network transfers as layers of an onion: lines, files, units, compression, restart markers, checksums. He wonders whether MODE, TYPE and STRU describe this adequately. The RFC is also a request for comments.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks every envelope and complains if one is damaged, out of order, the wrong size, or if the mail stops before the final description of the notebook.
